title: Doc2Quarto
text:
Overview
Doc2Quarto is a command-line utility written in Rust designed to streamline the migration of documentation projects from the Docusaurus framework to the Quarto publishing system.
Migrating large documentation sites can be painfully tedious. It often requiring manual adjustments to frontmatter, custom admonition syntax, and even directory structures.
Doc2Quarto automates these common, repetitive transformation tasks, allowing authors to focus on content updates.

title: Doc2Quarto
text:
1. Frontmatter
Docusaurus uses specific YAML fields like sidebar_position for navigation, which must be mapped to Quarto’s order field.

title: Doc2Quarto
text:
2. Admonitions:
Docusaurus uses the :::type Title syntax, while Quarto uses standardized Markdown Callouts (:::: {<type>} or :::: {.callout-<type>}).

title: Doc2Quarto
text:
3. File Structure:
Quarto books often use the .qmd extension and rely on a strict file hierarchy for book rendering.

title: Using the CLI
text:
Introduction
The Doc2Quarto utility is designed for straightforward command-line execution, requiring only the source directory of your existing Docusaurus documentation and a desired destination directory for the converted Quarto files.


Prerequisites
Doc2Quarto is built with Rust and packaged as a standalone binary. After installation (e.g., via cargo install), the doc2quarto command will be available in your system’s path.


Command Syntax



Help Command


The application uses the clap crate for argument parsing, defining two required arguments: --source and --dest.
The general command structure is:
$> doc2quarto -s <SOURCE_DIR> -d <DESTINATION_DIR>









Option
Long Name
Description
Example




-s
--source
The directory containing your Docusaurus .md files (the source docs root).
./my-docusaurus-docs/


-d
--dest
The directory where the converted .qmd files will be written. This directory will be created if it does not exist.
./quarto-book/chapters/


-h
--help
Print help
doc2-quarto —help


-v
--version
Prints Version
doc2quarto --version





Example Execution
Imagine your Docusaurus files are in a directory structure like this:
my-project/
├── docusaurus-docs/
│   ├── intro.md
│   └── guide/
│       ├── setup.md
│       └── images/
│           └── diagram.png
└── ...
To convert these files and place them into a new Quarto book structure:
$> doc2quarto --source docusaurus-docs --dest quarto-book/docs


During Execution

Validation: The tool checks that docusaurus-docs exists.
Creation: The destination directory quarto-book/docs is created.
Discovery: All .md files in docusaurus-docs are found recursively.
Conversion & Copying:

docusaurus-docs/intro.md is converted to quarto-book/docs/intro.qmd.
docusaurus-docs/guide/setup.md is converted to quarto-book/docs/guide/setup.qmd.
The docusaurus-docs/guide/images/ folder is copied to quarto-book/docs/guide/images/.

A progress bar provides visual feedback on the conversion process for large projects:

ℹ Found 25 markdown files
[✓] [########################################] 25/25 Processed: setup.md
Conversion completed!

The resulting Quarto files (.qmd) are then ready to be referenced in your main _quarto.yml file.



Example _quarto.yml configuration
project:
  type: book
book:
  title: "My Converted Book"
  chapters:
    - index.qmd
    - docs/intro.qmd
    - docs/guide/setup.qmd # Reference the converted files


Error Handling
Doc2Quarto includes checks for critical errors (as seen in main.rs):
If the source directory (-s) does not exist, the program will exit with an error.
If no .md files are found in the source directory, the program will exit.
The creation of the destination directory (-d) is handled gracefully; if it fails (due to permissions, for example), the program will report the error.

title: Conversion Logic
text:
Architecture
The core transformation logic of Doc2Quarto resides in the lib.rs file, primarily within the process_files and convert_content functions.
This chapter details how Docusaurus specific syntax is mapped to Quarto
This is a single pass pipeline for each file, ensuring efficient conversion.

title: Conversion Logic
text:
Admonitions
The conversion logic performs a mapping to ensure Docusaurus types correctly translate to Quarto’s built-in callout types:



Docusaurus
Quarto




:::note
:::: {note}


`:::tip`
`:::: {tip}`


`:::info`
`:::: {info}`


`:::caution`
`:::: {caution}`


`:::warning`
`:::: {warning}`


`:::danger`
`:::: {danger}`

title: Conversion Logic
text:
Example Conversion
A Docusaurus note with a title:
:::tip Useful Tip Remember to clear your cache after deployment.
:::
Is converted by Doc2Quarto into the Quarto syntax:
::: callout-tip
## Useful Tip
Remember to clear your cache after deployment.
:::

title: Introduction
text:
Neovim is fork of VI/VIM. It is brilliant, blazingly fast, highly configurable modal editor released in 2014. This repo helps you get started with using Neovim, giving you practical tips and providing necessary instructions to customise your IDE the way you want it.






Note



Vim/Neovim are called modal editors because their behavior changes depending on the working mode (Normal mode, Command mode, Visual mode, Visual Block mode etc)



History
Here’s the history of editors for the last 50 years. If you look at VI/VIM, it was release more than 4 decades ago and still used widely. VIM uses “VimL” or VimScript as scripting language where as Neovim uses a light weight, simple language called Lua.


Advantages
There are many IDEs like VSCode, Pycharm which just works out of the box then why Neovim? Some of the advantages are:-

Faster Navigation by eliminating the need of a mouse
Significantly improves your editing speed
Macros to automate repetitive tasks
Configure to your specific needs and preferences and stremline your workflow
You can have custom keybindings mapped to your frequently used commands
Enhance your productivity by providing features like split windows, quick search & replace and distraction-free mode too



Folder Structure
This is how the folder structure looks like. All the folders should be under $HOME/.config/nvim
~/.config/nvim/
├── init.lua              # Entry point: requires options, keymaps, and lazy
├── lazy-lock.json        # Auto-generated (DO NOT EDIT)
├── after/
│   └── ftplugin/
│       └── rust.lua      # Buffer-local settings for Rust
└── lua/
    ├── config/
    │   └── options.lua   # Core Neovim settings
    ├── keymaps.lua       # Global keymaps and .rsl detection
    └── plugins/
        ├── autopairs.lua # windwp/nvim-autopairs
        ├── gitsigns.lua  # lewis6991/gitsigns.nvim
        ├── lsp.lua       # Mason & non-Rust LSP configs
        ├── lualine.lua   # Project-aware Status Line (RUSTIMATE/COPE)
        ├── markdown.lua  # iamcco/markdown-preview.nvim
        ├── neogit.lua    # NeogitOrg/neogit (The Magit experience)
        ├── oil.lua       # stevearc/oil.nvim (Floating text-based explorer)
        ├── rustsetup.lua # mrcjkb/rustaceanvim (Deep Rust integration)
        ├── telescope.lua # nvim-telescope/telescope.nvim
        ├── theme.lua     # aliqyan-21/darkvoid.nvim
        └── ui.lua        # Undotree & toggleterm.nvim

init.lua
This is where nvim looks at everytime it starts so the lazy plugin manager is configured here. 


lazy-lock.json
This lock file helps you to configure neovim and the version quickly.


lua/plugins/
The best way to keep everything modularize is to split plugings into their own separate files and add it under this plugins directory. Lazy will automatically detect any changes on this folder and loads it.
Any/All plugin file should always return a table. Additional configuration/settings for that plugins should be inside a callback function. See the sample setup for lua/plugins/themes.lua. Same approach is used for most of the plugins unless specified differently in their documentation.
config = function() is a call back function. Look at the themes.lua file where the plugin is called and then colorscheme is setup.
return {
   "tiagovla/tokyodark.nvim",
   :
   :
   config = function()
      vim.cmd("colorscheme tokyodark")
   end
}

title: Plugins
text:
Core & UI Enhancements
This page serves as a reference for all Neovim plugins used in this configuration.

title: Plugins
text:
nvim-autopairs: Automatically closes brackets, quotes, and parentheses as soon as they are typed.
lualine.nvim: Provides a lightweight statusline showing Git status, current directory, file details, and mode status.
oil.nvim: A floating file manager that allows editing directory trees directly as a standard Neovim text buffer.
undotree: Displays a visual tree of buffer changes, making undo/redo history easy to navigate.
toggleterm.nvim: Provides floating, easily accessible terminal windows over editor splits.
darkvoid.nvim: Dark colorscheme applied across Neovim UI elements.

title: Plugins
text:
Language Support & LSP

mason.nvim & mason-lspconfig.nvim: Manages external binary installations for LSPs, formatters, and linters (lua_ls, pyright, bashls, html, cssls).
nvim-lspconfig: Configures native Neovim Language Server Protocol integrations and global keybindings for definitions, code actions, and rename floating windows.
rustaceanvim: Handles full Rust LSP setup with rust-analyzer, macro expansion, debugging capabilities via codelldb, and running inline tests.
nvim-treesitter: Provides code parsing for syntax highlighting, code structure evaluation, and custom language grammar integration (such as rustimate).
quarto.nvim & otter.nvim: Integrates Quarto rendering, interactive previews, and code chunk execution inside Markdown and .qmd files.

title: Plugins
text:
Git Integration

neogit: Interactive, floating Magit-style Git control dashboard.
gitsigns.nvim: Adds status signs in the gutter column for modified, added, or deleted lines.

title: Plugins
text:
Navigation

telescope.nvim: Highly customizable fuzzy finder for opening files, searching text across the project via live grep, listing buffers, and viewing help tags.

title: Configuration
text:
Package management
This chapter documents the configuration used to build my Emacs environment. It contains package management, the editor interface, completion, navigation and much more.
This emacs is setup for following programming language

title: Configuration
text:
Emacs uses package.el to manage packages.
Package archives such as GNU ELPA and MELPA provide packages. I use MELPA as an additional package archive and use-package to organize package configuration.
use-package groups related setup instructions for a package.
In this configuration, :ensure t is enabled by default so that packages are installed when needed.

;; We will be using package.el and load it to memory
(require 'package)

;; Add MELPA
(add-to-list 'package-archives
             '("melpa" . "https://melpa.org/packages/") t)

;; Initialize package system
(package-initialize)

;; Bootstrap use-package if not installed
;; use-package is built-in in newer Emacs versions
(unless (package-installed-p 'use-package)
  (package-refresh-contents)
  (package-install 'use-package))

;; Load use-package
(require 'use-package)

;; Always ensure packages are installed
;; This makes :ensure t the default for all use-package declarations
(setq use-package-always-ensure t)

title: Configuration
text:
Basics
The basic setup removes the menu and tool bars, enables mouse-wheel support and the tab bar, suppresses the startup messages, and configures line numbers , relative line numbers and recently opened files.
I use three text faces for fonts:

default for general text appearance
fixed-pitch for coding I use Iosevka
variable-pitch for prose

For default and fixed-pitch faces I use Iosevka and IBM Plex Sans prose (docs)
(menu-bar-mode -1)
(tool-bar-mode -1)
;; (scroll-bar-mode -1)
(mouse-wheel-mode 1)
(setq inhibit-startup-message t)
(setq inhibit-startup-echo-area-message t)
(tab-bar-mode 1)

;; Suppress harmless byte-compilation warning popups
(setq warning-minimum-level :error)

;; Do not take backup of any file
(setq make-backup-files nil)

;; Display line numbers and relative line numbers
(global-display-line-numbers-mode 1)
(setq display-line-numbers-type 'relative)

;; Remember recently opened files
;; Keybinding C-c C-r to open recent files
(recentf-mode 1)
(setq recentf-max-saved-items 100)

;; Default Monospace (Code & System)
(set-face-attribute 'default nil
                    :font "Iosevka"
                    :height 170)

(set-face-attribute 'fixed-pitch nil
                    :font "Iosevka"
                    :height 170)

;; Variable-Pitch (Prose & Org Text)
(set-face-attribute 'variable-pitch nil
                    :font "IBM Plex Sans"
                    :height 170)

;; Enable font-lock colors for Org mode
;; Enable global syntax highlighting where supported
(global-font-lock-mode 1)

;; Apply Variable-Pitch ONLY to Org default text
;; Keeps heading colors intact.
(custom-theme-set-faces
 'user
 '(org-default ((t (:inherit variable-pitch)))))

;; Theme setup
(use-package ef-themes
  :ensure t)

;; Primary Dark Theme
(load-theme 'ef-maris-dark t)

;; Secondary Light Theme
;; (load-theme 'ef-maris-light)

;; Theme switcher quick-reference (uncomment to switch)
;; (load-theme 'modus-vivendi t) ; High-contrast dark
;; (load-theme 'modus-operandi t) ; High-contrast light

title: Configuration
text:
Completion
The completion setup uses several packages together:

Vertico displays completion candidates vertically in the minibuffer.
Marginalia adds helpful descriptions alongside candidates.
Orderless allows matching terms in any order.
Consult provides search and navigation commands for lines, buffers, recent files, and projects.


Vertico
Vertico displays completion candidates vertically in the minibuffer. It is enabled globally.
(use-package vertico
  :init
  (vertico-mode 1))


Marginalia
Marginalia adds helpful information next to completion candidates and works with Vertico.
(use-package marginalia
  :init
  (marginalia-mode 1))


Orderless
Orderless provides matching in any order. The completion-styles setting uses both orderless and basic. The configuration also clears the default category settings and specifies matching styles for files.
(use-package orderless
  :custom
  (completion-styles '(orderless basic))
  (completion-category-defaults nil)
  (completion-category-overrides '((file (styles basic partial-completion)))))


Consult
Consult provides search and navigation commands for files, buffers, lines, and project content. The project-wide search commands require ripgrep to be installed.
(use-package consult
  :bind (;; Search commands
         ("C-s" . consult-line)              ; Search in current buffer
         ("C-x b" . consult-buffer)          ; Switch buffer with preview
         ;; File navigation
         ("C-x C-r" . consult-recent-file)   ; Recent files
         ;; Project-wide search (requires ripgrep installed)
         ("C-c s g" . consult-ripgrep)       ; Grep in project
         ("C-c s f" . consult-find))         ; Find file in project
  :config
  ;; Preview files/buffers as you navigate (optional)
  (setq consult-preview-key 'any))

title: Configuration
text:
In-buffer completion
Corfu provides an in-buffer completion popup. It is an alternative to Company mode and displays completion suggestions at the cursor. In this setup, Corfu works with Eglot, Cape, and Emacs completion facilities.

Corfu
The configuration enables Corfu globally, turns on automatic completion, sets the delay and minimum prefix length, enables cycling, and configures popup information. The keybindings below apply to corfu-map.
(use-package corfu
  :init
  (global-corfu-mode 1)
  ;; :hook (rust-ts-mode . cargo-minor-mode)
  :custom
  (corfu-auto t)
  (corfu-auto-delay 0.2)
  (corfu-auto-prefix 2)
  (corfu-cycle t)
  (corfu-popupinfo-delay 0.5)
  :bind (:map corfu-map
              ("TAB" . corfu-next)
              ([tab] . corfu-next)
              ("S-TAB" . corfu-previous)
              ([backtab] . corfu-previous)
              ("M-d" . corfu-popupinfo-toggle))
  :config
  ;; Enable documentation popup next to completion candidates
  (corfu-popupinfo-mode 1))


Cape
Cape provides additional completion-at-point backends that can be used by the completion system. This configuration adds file, dabbrev, and Emacs Lisp block completion functions to completion-at-point-functions.
(use-package cape
  :init
  ;; Add completion backends at startup
  (add-to-list 'completion-at-point-functions #'cape-file)
  (add-to-list 'completion-at-point-functions #'cape-dabbrev)
  ;; Add Elisp completion even in this Org file
  (add-to-list 'completion-at-point-functions #'cape-elisp-block))

title: Configuration
text:
Language support
The language-support setup uses Eglot as the LSP client, Eldoc for documentation display, and Tree-sitter-based Rust mode. It also configures language servers for JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, and enables Eglot for shell scripts.

Eglot and Eldoc
Eglot is built into Emacs in the version used by this configuration, so :ensure nil is specified. eglot-workspace-configuration passes settings to language servers. The example below sets the Rust Analyzer check command to check.
;; Eldoc: Minibuffer documentation display
(use-package eldoc
  :ensure nil
  :custom
  (eldoc-echo-area-use-multiline-p nil))

;; Eglot: Lightweight LSP client
(use-package eglot
  :ensure nil  ; Built-in from Emacs 29+
  :custom
  (eglot-autoshutdown t)
  (eglot-extend-to-xref t)
  :config
  ;; Format on save when Eglot is managing the current buffer
  (add-hook 'before-save-hook
            (lambda ()
              (when (eglot-managed-p)
                (eglot-format-buffer))))

  ;; Configure language-server workspace settings
  (setq-default eglot-workspace-configuration
                '((:rust-analyzer . ((check . ((command . "check"))))))))

(add-to-list 'eglot-server-programs
             '(js-mode "typescript-language-server" "--stdio"))


Rust with TS
The Rust setup uses rust-ts-mode, Eglot, and Cargo. It adds a Tree-sitter (TS) grammar search path and specifies the Rust grammar source. Enables Eglot and cargo-minor-mode when rust-ts-mode starts.
The keybindings provide navigation between Flymake diagnostics and Cargo build, run, test, and check commands.
;; Check for additional Tree-sitter grammar in the path below
(add-to-list 'treesit-extra-load-path
             (expand-file-name "tree-sitter" user-emacs-directory))

;; Configure Tree-sitter grammar source (ABI v14 compatible)
(setq treesit-language-source-alist
      '((rust "https://github.com/tree-sitter/tree-sitter-rust" "v0.21.2")))

;; Enable Tree-sitter Rust mode
(use-package rust-ts-mode
  :ensure nil
  :mode "\\.rs\\'"
  :init
  ;; Maximum syntax highlighting level for Tree-sitter
  (setq treesit-font-lock-level 4)
  :hook ((rust-ts-mode . eglot-ensure)
         (rust-ts-mode . cargo-minor-mode))
  :bind (:map rust-ts-mode-map
         ("M-n" . flymake-goto-next-error)
         ("M-p" . flymake-goto-prev-error)
         ("C-c c b" . cargo-process-build)
         ("C-c c r" . cargo-process-run)
         ("C-c c t" . cargo-process-test)
         ("C-c c k" . cargo-process-check))
  :custom
  (rust-ts-mode-indent-offset 4))

;; Cargo execution runner
(use-package cargo
  :ensure t)


HTML, CSS, and JS
The following configuration adds language-server commands for HTML and CSS after Eglot has loaded. The JavaScript server mapping is configured above in the Eglot section.
(with-eval-after-load 'eglot
  (add-to-list 'eglot-server-programs
               '(mhtml-mode "vscode-html-language-server" "--stdio"))
  (add-to-list 'eglot-server-programs
               '(css-mode "vscode-css-language-server" "--stdio")))
Run local server with the following command:
python3 -m http.server 8000


Shell scripting
The shell setup associates .sh, .bash, and .zsh files with sh-mode and starts Eglot when sh-mode is enabled.
(use-package sh-script
  :ensure nil
  :mode (("\\.sh\\'" . sh-mode)
         ("\\.bash\\'" . sh-mode)
         ("\\.zsh\\'" . sh-mode))
  :hook (sh-mode . eglot-ensure))

title: Configuration
text:
Sessions
Emacs has a built-in desktop feature for restoring a previous session. This is stored in a sessions/ directory inside user-emacs-directory. It enables desktop-save-mode, and sets automatic saving so that no prompt is required.
;; Use a sessions directory inside the Emacs configuration folder
(setq desktop-dirname
      (expand-file-name "sessions/" user-emacs-directory))

(setq desktop-path (list desktop-dirname))

(desktop-save-mode 1)
;; Ensure it is always true so no prompt is required
(setq desktop-save t)
